name: Grace Javier Alfonso
half: Grace Javier Alfonso has advised eight theses in this repository between 2018 and 2024. Their supervision record covers a diverse range of communication-related fields, with a notable emphasis on communication studies, public health and COVID-19, and arts and creative practice, each appearing three times in their advised list. Governance and public policy topics appear twice, while journalism and news media also feature in two supervised works. Additional interests include culture and identity, gender and inclusion, and agriculture and food, each represented by a single thesis. The research topics suggest a focus on how communication intersects with social issues, crisis management, and community development. For instance, one 2024 thesis examined communication dynamics and safety culture onboard Seabourn Cruises, while another explored geospatial direct-address videos as tools for participatory governance in Laguna. Earlier work includes an investigation into radio-based instruction during the pandemic and an analysis of humor in ASEAN stand-up comedy as a coping mechanism during crises. Alfonso also supervised studies on filmmaking as a tool for trauma recovery among typhoon survivors and the role of mass media in transforming marginalized Cordilleran communities. The 2018 theses focused on risk communication regarding mercury in small-scale mining and intergenerational communication among women rice farmers in Northern Samar. While Alfonso has no advisees recorded for 2026, with the latest advisee year being 2024, they remain an active presence in the repository with items listed up to 2026. Their profile indicates a strong capacity to guide students in qualitative and narrative inquiry methods, particularly those examining the intersection of media, culture, and public policy. The breadth of topics suggests flexibility in supervising interdisciplinary projects that blend communication theory with practical social applications.

The other 2024 thesis, by Ivan Khalil L. Descartin, explored governance and public policy through the lens of arts and creative practice. This project highlighted an innovative approach to civic engagement by merging digital media with local decision-making processes.

Previous years show a focus on media’s role in crisis and community transformation. In 2023, Crisanto E. Avila’s thesis examined radio-based instruction as an alternative learning modality during the COVID-19 pandemic, linking journalism and news media with public health responses. In 2022, two theses were completed. Kerchlynn C. Tan’s work used narrative inquiry to explore how Super Typhoon Yolanda survivors in Leyte confronted emotional trauma through filmmaking, emphasizing arts and creative practice as a mechanism for psychosocial wellness. Mavin David S. Catbagan’s thesis analyzed stand-up comedy in ASEAN countries as a socio-cultural coping mechanism during the crisis, combining arts, public health, and governance themes through textual analysis of online videos.

Earlier work includes Maria Rica A. Lumangcas’s 2021 study on how a prime time TV series transformed a Cordilleran community, focusing on journalism and media’s impact on socio-economic change and identity. The 2018 entries reveal an interest in marginalized voices and risk communication. Salvie S. Magtanao’s dissertation examined intergenerational communication among women rice farmers in Northern Samar, addressing gender, agriculture, and resistance. Another 2018 thesis by an unnamed author analyzed communication materials regarding mercury risks in small-scale mining, utilizing critical discourse analysis. These works demonstrate a consistent engagement with social issues, media effectiveness, and community narratives. Alfonso’s supervision pattern suggests a preference for qualitative methods, including autoethnography, narrative inquiry, and textual analysis. The range of topics indicates flexibility in guiding students through diverse intersections of communication, policy, and cultural practice.
